title: SpaceX Got Approval for 1 Million Satellites. Can Data Centers in Space Actually Work?

scenes.narration: The day before Thanksgiving, America's telecoms regulator gave one company permission to launch a million satellites. Not for internet. For artificial intelligence. So why would anyone put data centers in space, and does the maths actually work?

On November twenty-fifth, the Federal Communications Commission granted SpaceX authority for a constellation it calls Starmind. Up to one million satellites, each one a small data center, running AI in low Earth orbit.

props.headline: FCC authorizes SpaceX's Starmind: up to 1,000,000 satellites operating as data centers in space
props.dek: Order DA 26-1273, granted in part, with conditions

scenes.narration: For scale: there are roughly sixteen to seventeen thousand working satellites in orbit today, depending on who's counting. The tracker Orbital Radar puts it at about sixteen thousand seven hundred, according to CNN. Starmind alone would be about sixty times that.

props.label: Working satellites in orbit today
props.note: Orbital Radar, via CNN. ESA counts 15,800.

scenes.narration: FCC chairman Brendan Carr, as quoted by CNN, called it a bold new frontier. Elon Musk replied on X: much appreciated, this will be a great asset to America and the world.

props.text: This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth.
props.author: Brendan Carr

scenes.narration: But what did the FCC actually sign off on? The fine print is more interesting than the headline.

Strictly speaking, the FCC licenses radio, not computers. According to the order itself, the grant covers the backup and emergency radio links used to track and command the satellites. They'll fly in thin orbital shells between five hundred and about a thousand kilometres up, on a fifteen-year licence.

props.title: What the order covers
items: Licence for backup and emergency radio links

scenes.narration: And it comes with deadlines. SpaceX's prospectus says it hopes to start launching as early as twenty twenty-eight. The FCC says the licence is void unless one satellite is working by November twenty thirty-three, a hundred thousand by twenty thirty-five, half the fleet by twenty thirty-eight, and all of it by twenty forty.

events.text: SpaceX's target for first compute satellites
Full constellation, or the licence is void

scenes.narration: The order also sets conditions. SpaceX wanted to send dead satellites above six hundred kilometres into disposal orbits, or off around the sun, instead of burning them up in the atmosphere. The FCC put that on hold until SpaceX gives more detail. It did waive the surety bond, the deposit operators normally post to show they're serious.

props.title: The fine print
items: Disposal plan above 600 km: on hold

scenes.narration: And the FCC set aside objections about the environment and about astronomy, saying they're outside its authority. We'll come back to who raised them.

props.text: We dismiss comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns.
props.author: FCC Space Bureau

scenes.narration: To understand why anyone wants this, look down at the ground, and at what AI is doing to the electricity grid.

According to the International Energy Agency, data centres used about four hundred and fifteen terawatt hours of electricity in twenty twenty-four. That's around one and a half percent of all the world's electricity. By twenty thirty, the agency expects that to more than double, to around nine hundred and forty-five.

props.title: Data centre electricity use (TWh)
props.source: IEA, Energy and AI (2025), base case

scenes.narration: The fastest-growing part is AI itself. The IEA expects electricity demand from data centres built for AI to more than quadruple by twenty thirty.

props.label: Growth in AI data-centre power demand by 2030

scenes.narration: Most of that growth is in two countries. The IEA says the United States and China account for nearly eighty percent of it.

props.title: Nearly 80% of data-centre demand growth
props.source: IEA, Energy and AI (2025), growth to 2030

scenes.narration: And building on the ground is getting harder politically. According to CBS News, in this month's midterm elections American voters approved dozens of proposals aimed at restricting data centers.

props.title: Why the ground is getting harder
items: Electricity demand set to double by 2030
Growth concentrated in the US and China

scenes.narration: SpaceX's pitch is simple. Go somewhere the sun almost never sets, and nobody lives next door.

Above the atmosphere there are no clouds, and in the right orbit, almost no night. Google's researchers, who are working on their own version of this idea, say a solar panel in the right orbit can be up to eight times more productive than on Earth.

props.label: Solar output in the right orbit vs. on Earth
props.note: 'Up to', according to Google's Project Suncatcher team

scenes.narration: SpaceX says it will fly a dawn-dusk orbit, riding the line between day and night so the panels stay in near-constant sunlight. In its application, as quoted by CNN, the company said that would bring transformative cost and energy efficiency.

props.text: By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency.
props.author: SpaceX

scenes.narration: Each satellite, as described by New Atlas, would span about seventy metres, with a rack of radiation-hardened computers in the middle, flanked by a solar array and a radiator. SpaceX's prospectus says early satellites will carry around a hundred kilowatts of computing power each.

props.title: One Starmind satellite
items: Solar array: up to 250 kW peak

scenes.narration: And the ambition is enormous. SpaceX says its goal is to put one hundred gigawatts of computing power into orbit every year. By its own estimate, that would take thousands of launches a year, and around a million metric tons of cargo.

props.label: SpaceX's goal: AI compute launched to orbit, per year

scenes.narration: All of that hinges on one number: what it costs to lift a kilogram into orbit.

By NASA's figures, the Space Shuttle cost about fifty-four thousand dollars for every kilogram it carried to low Earth orbit. SpaceX's Falcon 9 brought the advertised price down to about two thousand seven hundred. Falcon Heavy, about fourteen hundred.

props.title: Cost to low Earth orbit ($ per kg)

scenes.narration: SpaceX says Starship, its fully reusable rocket, is meant to cut the cost of reaching orbit by ninety-nine percent or more, compared with the historical average. If it gets there, that's under two hundred dollars a kilo.

props.title: Starship's cost target
props.note: '99% or more' lower, according to SpaceX

scenes.narration: That's the number that matters. Google's analysis says launch prices could fall below two hundred dollars a kilogram by the mid twenty-thirties. At that price, it says, launching and running a space data center could cost roughly the same as just the energy bill of a similar one on Earth.

props.label: Google's launch-price threshold, mid-2030s
props.note: Compared with a ground data centre's energy costs only

scenes.narration: SpaceX itself admits the whole idea depends on Starship. Its prospectus puts it plainly.

props.text: AI compute satellites at scale need full Starship reusability to be economically compelling.
props.author: SpaceX

scenes.narration: But even if launches get cheap, there's a problem money can't wish away. Heat.
On Earth, data centres carry heat away with air and water. In a vacuum there's no air. The only way to get rid of heat is to radiate it away, and that takes surface area. A lot of it.

props.title: Cooling in a vacuum
items: No air or water to carry heat away
Heat must be radiated into space
More heat means more radiator area

scenes.narration: An analysis in IEEE Spectrum, by Andrew Cavalier of ABI Research, found that one high-end AI chip, kept at sixty degrees, needs about one point four square metres of radiator. After five years of wear, nearly two.

props.label: Radiator area for one 700-watt AI chip
props.note: At 60 °C; nearly 2.0 m² after five years (ABI Research)

scenes.narration: Scale that up, and by the same analysis a single server rack needs a radiator of about eighty square metres. Roughly the size of a badminton court.

props.label: Radiator needed for one server rack

scenes.narration: Add the cost of launch and radiation-proofing, and that model found running a chip in space for a year cost at least ten times more than on the ground. And that was assuming launches at just forty-four dollars a kilo. Its conclusion:

props.text: The cost of delivery and space hardening of the payload makes general-purpose space-based data centers difficult to justify economically today.
props.author: Andrew Cavalier

scenes.narration: And then there are the people who tried to stop it.
Three groups formally asked the FCC to deny the application. Amazon, through its own satellite internet business, Amazon Leo. The satellite operator Viasat. And the American Astronomical Society.

Amazon, a direct competitor, called Starmind a lofty ambition rather than a real plan, according to CNBC's account of its filing, and said it would take SpaceX centuries to build. Amazon declined to comment on the approval.

props.text: A lofty ambition rather than a real plan.
props.author: Amazon (Kuiper Systems)

scenes.narration: Astronomers are worried about the night sky. According to CNN, the American Astronomical Society said it was dismayed, warning the satellites would be visible as extremely bright objects, and would threaten sensitive research instruments.

props.text: Extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky.
props.author: American Astronomical Society

scenes.narration: Environmental lawyers object too. CNBC reports that Earthjustice criticised the FCC for deciding during a holiday week, and without the environmental review it says federal law requires. The FCC's position is that those questions are outside its authority.
Whatever the objections, SpaceX isn't the only one making this bet.

Last November, a startup called Starcloud flew an Nvidia H100, a data-centre AI chip, on a SpaceX rocket, and later said it had trained a small language model in orbit. In March, according to CNBC, Blue Origin asked for up to fifty-one thousand six hundred satellites. Google put its first AI chips in space in October, and plans two prototypes with Planet by early twenty twenty-seven.

events.text: Starcloud flies an Nvidia H100 in orbit
Blue Origin seeks up to 51,600 satellites
Google's first AI chips reach orbit

scenes.narration: And SpaceX has public money behind it now. Its June IPO raised a record seventy-five billion dollars, valuing the company at about one point eight trillion.

props.label: Raised in SpaceX's June IPO, a record
props.note: Valued at about $1.77 trillion at pricing

scenes.narration: But the same prospectus is candid about the risk. It warns that orbital AI compute involves

props.text: Unproven technologies or technologies that do not exist, and such initiatives may not achieve commercial viability.
props.author: SpaceX

scenes.narration: So what should you watch for next?

Four things. First, whether Starship becomes fully reusable, because SpaceX itself says the economics depend on it. Second, the twenty twenty-eight target for the first compute satellites. Third, the disposal plan for satellites above six hundred kilometres, which still needs FCC approval. And fourth, the hard deadline: a hundred thousand satellites by twenty thirty-five, or the licence is void.

A million data centers in the sky is either the next great infrastructure build, or the most expensive way ever devised to cool a computer. The deadlines will tell us which. Subscribe so you don't miss the next one.
